what_its_for: Itraconazole is an antifungal medicine used to treat fungal infections. It can treat infections in your lungs, nails, mouth, throat, and other parts of your body. Common infections it treats include toenail or fingernail fungus (onychomycosis), histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, and aspergillosis.
how_to_take: Take itraconazole exactly as your doctor tells you. Capsules and tablets should be taken WITH a full meal to help your body absorb the medicine properly. Swallow capsules and tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. The liquid (oral solution) works differently — take it on an EMPTY STOMACH, swish it around in your mouth before swallowing. Take your doses at the same time each day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your dose depends on the type of infection being treated and which form of itraconazole you are taking. Typical doses range from 100 mg to 400 mg per day, taken once or twice daily. Nail fungus is often treated for 3 to 6 months. Other infections may require shorter or longer courses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store itraconazole at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid oral solution at room temperature and do not refrigerate or freeze it. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking itraconazole with certain medicines as it can cause serious or life-threatening interactions. Do NOT take it with certain cholesterol medicines (like lovastatin or simvastatin), certain sedatives (like triazolam or oral midazolam), certain heart rhythm medicines (like quinidine or dofetilide), or certain migraine medicines (like ergotamine). Avoid drinking grapefruit juice as it can affect how the medicine works. Avoid alcohol as it may increase the risk of liver problems. Tell ALL your doctors and your pharmacist about every medicine, vitamin, supplement, or herbal product you take before starting itraconazole.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe stomach pain or nausea, unusual tiredness or weakness (possible signs of liver problems), chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling of your legs or feet (possible heart problems), severe skin rash, blistering or peeling skin, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: Itraconazole starts working soon after you begin taking it, but it may take several weeks or even months before you notice improvement, especially for nail infections. Nail fungus treatment can take 3 to 6 months, and you may not see fully healthy nails until new nail growth comes in, which can take up to a year. For other fungal infections, you may start to feel better within a few weeks. Always finish your full course of treatment even if you feel better, to make sure the infection is completely gone.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not take itraconazole if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it may harm your unborn baby. Women of childbearing age should use effective birth control during treatment and for 2 months after stopping. Breastfeeding: Itraconazole passes into breast milk — talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Use in children should only be under close medical supervision. Older adults: Older patients may need closer monitoring for side effects, especially liver and heart-related effects. Kidney or liver disease: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you.
